title: Unauthenticated basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded and is not authenticated before being passed to pickle.loads. An attacker can send a crafted cookie whose pickle payload executes arbitrary Python code in the application process during any request that reads the basket.

title: Order details can be read by any authenticated customer
description: show_order loads an order by the supplied ID but never checks that it belongs to the authenticated user. Any customer who can guess or learn another order ID can read its status, prices, items, payment totals, and refunds.

title: Product search concatenates the query into SQL
description: The public search parameter is inserted directly into a SQL statement. SQL metacharacters can change the query and potentially expose or modify database data, depending on the SQLite statement context.
evidence: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50"

title: Customer-controlled display names reach an admin SQL query
description: A customer can set display_name through the account endpoint, and the reports endpoint interpolates that value into SQL. A malicious customer name can therefore inject SQL when staff request the review report for that customer.
evidence: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC"

title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, but the product template renders it with the safe filter. A reviewer can store markup or script that executes for visitors to the product page, including staff or other customers.

title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
description: The application uses a source-controlled constant as the HS256 signing key. Anyone who obtains the repository can mint valid tokens for arbitrary users, including staff users, and access all bearer-token protected functionality.

title: Token refresh trusts an unsigned user identity
description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and then issues a signed token for the user ID in the attacker-supplied claims. User IDs are sequential, so an attacker can submit an unsigned token naming another account and obtain a valid token for that account (including staff).
evidence: claims = jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}); user = load_user(claims.get("sub")); return jsonify(token=make_token(user))

title: Authentication failures are swallowed by the auth decorator
description: abort(401) raises an exception that is caught by the broad handler, after which the protected view is still called with g.user set to None. This bypasses the intended authentication gate; the gift-card balance view then returns data without using g.user, allowing unauthenticated balance lookups when a card code is known.
evidence: except Exception: ... g.user = None; return f(*args, **kwargs)

title: Payment-status timeout is treated as successful payment
description: If the payment provider times out, the endpoint fails open by setting status to paid and processing the order without receiving confirmation. A customer can cause or exploit provider/network timeouts to obtain fulfillment without a verified payment.

title: Webhook signature does not cover the event payload
description: The HMAC authenticates only the order ID, not the status or amount. Anyone able to obtain or replay a valid signature for an order can alter amount_pence or status while retaining the same signature, allowing an order to be marked paid for an arbitrary amount. In the supplied production config, the fallback webhook secret is also a source-visible constant.
evidence: webhook_signature(order_id) signs only str(order_id); event status and amount_pence are accepted separately; config.py defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to whsec-local

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashes use a fast, unsalted general-purpose hash. A database compromise permits efficient offline cracking and identical passwords produce identical hashes; a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a unique salt is required for resistant storage.
